title: Task-Optimized Convolutional Recurrent Networks Align with Tactile Process

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states 'moderate correlation between supervised categorization performance and neural alignment' but Figure 5b shows r = 0.60 (also stated as r = 0.59 in the text), which is typically considered a moderate-to-strong correlation, not merely moderate. The abstract's characterization appears to understate the finding.

The text states 'The best-performing model is Zhuang+GPT+Supervised (rightmost cyan bar)' in Figure 3 caption, but the figure shows multiple bars and it's unclear which specific bar represents this model. The color coding and labeling in Figure 3 do not clearly identify a 'rightmost cyan bar' as the best performer.

The text states 'The mean animal-to-animal score is 0.18' in the Methods section under Neural Data Comparison, but in Appendix A4 it states 'We found the mean pooled animal score was 0.175'. These should be the same value but differ (0.18 vs 0.175).

The appendix reports 'mean pooled animal score was 0.175 with a s.e.m. of 0.161 and maximum score of 1.34'. A maximum score of 1.34 for a correlation metric (RSA Pearson's r) is impossible, as Pearson correlation coefficients are bounded between -1 and 1. This suggests either a reporting error or the metric is not actually a standard correlation.

Figure 4b caption states 'The mean animal-to-animal score is 0.18 and the maximum between all pairs of animals is 0.34', but the text in Results refers to models 'exceeding the average inter-animal neural consistency (leftmost black "a2a" bar in Fig. 4b)' and later states models 'saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance'. However, several models in Figure 4b appear to exceed 0.34 (the stated maximum), which is contradictory.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results Section 4, paragraph on ConvRNN Encoders
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'the SimCLR-trained EAD with the IntersectionRNN encoder best matches the neural data with far fewer parameters (~3.80 × 10^7 parameters) than its supervised counterpart with a GPT-based attender (~6.38 × 10^7 parameters)'. However, earlier it states 'the SimCLR-optimized Intersection RNN EAD achieved the best absolute neural alignment score across all models overall', but Figure 4b shows multiple models with similar or higher scores, creating ambiguity about which model truly has the 'best' score.

The text states 'we extract 22 timesteps for both datasets, corresponding to the average whisking frequency of 20 Hz in rodents'. However, 22 timesteps at 20 Hz would correspond to 1.1 seconds of data, but the neural data description states trials last 'about 1–2 seconds'. The correspondence between simulation timesteps and real whisking frequency is unclear and potentially inconsistent.

The abstract claims 'contrastive self-supervised ConvRNN-encoder-based EADs... match supervised neural fits', but in Results it states the SimCLR model 'was comparable in its neural alignment to its supervised... variant' and achieved 'the best absolute neural alignment score'. The word 'match' in the abstract could be interpreted as equal performance, but 'best' and 'comparable' suggest slight differences that may not constitute a true 'match'.

Table 6 shows decoding accuracies for shape and distance. For 'Resnet+Mamba+SimCLR', the shape decoding is exactly at chance (0.50), which seems suspiciously low given that other models exceed chance. This could indicate a training or evaluation error for this specific model, or the model failed to learn shape-relevant features despite having good neural fit (0.70).

predicted_errors.error_location: Results Section 4, paragraph on neural alignment
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims models 'saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance' and 'robustly passing the NeuroAI Turing Test'. However, the test involves only 6 stimuli (concave/convex × 3 distances) which is acknowledged as a 'critical limitation'. Claiming to have 'saturated' explainable variance and 'robustly passed' a test with such limited stimulus diversity overstates the generalizability of the findings.
